g6-bridging-w2-core.prompt: Goal: persuade Grade 6 students to join the chess club. The prompt was: "Write 4 sentences about the chess club for Grade 6 students." The output was 4 clear sentences saying when and where the club meets, but it did not try to persuade anyone to join. Judging the output against the goal, which weakness should you name before writing v2?
options: The prompt never says what the writing should do, so the AI just described the club instead of persuading.
The prompt never says who will read it, so the AI wrote for the wrong audience.
The prompt never sets a length, so the AI did not know how much to write.
The prompt contains too many words, so the AI got confused about the topic.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the audience and the length were already in the prompt, so the missing piece was the task itself: 'persuade' was never asked for.
feedback.incorrect: Re-read the prompt: it already names Grade 6 students and asks for 4 sentences, so the gap is the task - it never tells the AI to persuade.

g6-bridging-w2-core.prompt: Sara wants a better notice from her prompt. Put her actions in the order of the refinement loop taught in this lesson.
items: She writes v2, changing only the one weakness she named.
She decides what the notice must achieve and writes that goal down.
She judges the v2 output against the same goal to see if it improved.
She reads the v1 output and compares it with her goal.
She names the one weakness that best explains the gap.

feedback.correct: That is the loop: set the goal, judge, name the weakness, make one change, then re-judge against the same goal.
feedback.incorrect: The goal comes first because you cannot judge an output without one, and the weakness must be named before you know what to change.

g6-bridging-w2-core.prompt: Goal: a science-fair notice that Grade 3 students can read on their own. The prompt was "Write a notice about the science fair." The output was correct but used long words like 'methodology' and 'apparatus'. Which changes to the prompt would target that weakness? Choose all that apply.
options: Add: "Write it for Grade 3 students."
Add: "Use short sentences and words an 8-year-old knows."
Add: "Include the date, time and room of the fair."
Add: "Make it 200 words instead of 100."
Add: "Use a formal tone suitable for the school principal."

feedback.correct: Both changes tell the AI who is reading and how to write for them, which is exactly the weakness you named.
feedback.incorrect: The weakness was the reading level, so only changes about the audience or the words used will fix it - adding details, more length or a formal tone does not.

g6-bridging-w2-core.prompt: A student changes the audience, the length and the format of a prompt all at once, and the new output is much better. She can be sure which of those three changes made it better.

feedback.correct: Right - with three changes at once the improvement could come from any of them, which is why refiners change one thing at a time.
feedback.incorrect: A better output only proves that something helped; changing one thing at a time is what lets you say which change caused it.

g6-bridging-w2-core.prompt: Each output below missed the goal in a different way. Match the problem with the single change to the prompt that targets it.
left: The notice used words the Grade 3 class could not read.
The answer filled two pages when a short notice was wanted.
The answer came back as one long paragraph when a list was needed.
The answer was about the wrong school event entirely.
right: State the exact event the writing is about.
Name who will be reading it.
Ask for the output as a bulleted list.
Set a limit, such as four sentences.

feedback.correct: Each fix targets one named weakness - audience, constraint, format or an ambiguous task - which is why you can tell what caused the improvement.
feedback.incorrect: Name the weakness first, then pick the change that speaks to it: a reading-level problem needs an audience, and a too-long answer needs a limit.

g6-bridging-w2-lab.prompt: A team iterates a prompt from v1 to v4. Because v4 is the newest version, it must be the team's best-balanced version.

feedback.correct: Right - a later change can cost you on one goal, so the best balance is the version your log shows fits the purpose, not simply the last one.
feedback.incorrect: Each version changes one thing, and a change can help clarity while hurting accuracy - so v4 is best only if the log shows it balances both goals for your purpose.

g6-bridging-w2-lab.prompt:
A team iterated a notice about the school recycling drive, one change per version, and scored each output out of 5 for clarity and accuracy.
v1 "Write about the recycling drive." - clarity 2, accuracy 3
v2 added "write it in 4 sentences" - clarity 4, accuracy 3
v3 added "for Grade 3 readers" - clarity 5, accuracy 1 (the collection dates disappeared)
v4 added "include the collection dates" - clarity 4, accuracy 4
Match each version with what its log entry shows.
left: v2: added "write it in 4 sentences"
v3: added "for Grade 3 readers"
v4: added "include the collection dates"
v1: "Write about the recycling drive."
right: Brought a true detail back, costing a little clarity.
Made the notice clearer and left accuracy exactly as it was.
The starting point, with nothing yet to compare it against.
Gave the clearest output of all, but a true detail was lost.

feedback.correct: Because only one thing changed each time, every row of the log can be read as the cause of that version's effect.
feedback.incorrect: Compare each version's two scores with the version before it: that difference is the effect of the one change made in that version.

g6-bridging-w2-lab.prompt: Using the same log (v1 clarity 2 / accuracy 3; v2 clarity 4 / accuracy 3; v3 clarity 5 / accuracy 1; v4 clarity 4 / accuracy 4): v3’s accuracy score is how many points lower than v2’s?

feedback.correct: Accuracy fell from 3 to 1, so the clearer v3 cost 2 accuracy points - that number is the size of the trade-off.
feedback.incorrect: Subtract v3's accuracy score from v2's: 3 - 1 = 2. Measuring the loss is how you show a trade-off with evidence instead of just claiming one.

g6-bridging-w2-lab.prompt: Using the same log (v1 clarity 2 / accuracy 3; v2 clarity 4 / accuracy 3; v3 clarity 5 / accuracy 1, dates dropped; v4 clarity 4 / accuracy 4), which statements does the log actually support? Choose all that apply.
options: v2's change raised clarity without changing accuracy.
v3's change raised clarity but lowered accuracy.
v4 is the only version scoring 4 or more on both goals.
Every version after v1 improved both goals.
v3 lost accuracy because the team changed two things in that version.

feedback.correct: You read the log as evidence: two of the changes helped one goal only, and just one version reaches 4 on both.
feedback.incorrect: Check each claim against the numbers - v3's accuracy fell, so not every version improved both goals, and the log records only one change per version.

g6-bridging-w2-lab.prompt: The notice will be handed to Grade 3 students and it must tell them the correct collection dates. Using the same log (v1 clarity 2 / accuracy 3; v2 clarity 4 / accuracy 3; v3 clarity 5 / accuracy 1, dates dropped; v4 clarity 4 / accuracy 4), which choice of best-balanced version is best justified by the evidence?
options: v4, because it keeps clarity high at 4 while bringing the correct dates back.
v3, because it scored highest of all the versions on clarity.
v2, because it was the first version that improved on v1.
v1, because it was written before any goal pulled against another.

feedback.correct: The purpose needs both goals, and v4 is the only version the log shows meeting both - a clear notice that still carries the right dates.
feedback.incorrect: Judge against the purpose: a notice missing the collection dates fails its job however clear it reads, so the highest clarity score alone cannot justify the choice.

g6-bridging-w1-core.prompt: A team trains an AI to spot dates in photos. Every photo and label is correct except one: a photo of a small grey stone has been labelled "date". Which mistake should you predict in the AI's output?

options.text: It will sometimes look at a small grey stone and call it a date.
It will refuse to answer whenever it is shown a stone.
It will start calling real dates stones.
It will be unaffected, because one wrong photo is too small a part of the dataset to matter.

feedback.correct: Right - the model copies the pattern in its examples, so one stone labelled "date" teaches it that a small grey lump can be a date, and it says so confidently.
feedback.incorrect: Follow the chain from the data: the stone was labelled "date", so the model learns that shape counts as a date and applies that lesson to new stones.

g6-bridging-w1-core.prompt: A team has 40 date photos that are clear and correctly labelled. They add 4,000 more photos, but many labels in that new batch are wrong. Select every statement that is a good prediction of what happens.

options.text: The dataset is now much bigger, but lower in quality.
The wrong pattern will be taught more strongly than before, because far more examples now repeat it.
Knowing only that the dataset grew does not tell you the outputs will be better.
The outputs will improve, because the AI now has far more examples to learn from.
The new photos cannot do any harm, because the 40 correct photos are still in the set.

feedback.correct: Yes - quantity and quality are different things, and a huge dataset full of mistakes just teaches the wrong pattern more strongly.
feedback.incorrect: More data only helps if the data is good: adding thousands of wrong labels repeats the wrong lesson, and the correct 40 cannot cancel that out.

g6-bridging-w1-core.prompt: Four teams trained the same AI on different versions of a date-photo dataset. Match each dataset to the output you should expect from it.

left.text: A few stones are labelled "date"; everything else is correct.
Every photo is correct, but the set contains only dark brown dates - no yellow ones.
Half the photos are blurry and the labels are written as "date", "dat" and "DATE".
Only 12 photos, but all clear, all correctly labelled, and covering every kind of date.

right.text: It confidently calls small stones dates.
It handles brown dates well but gets yellow dates wrong, because it never saw one.
It is unsure and inconsistent on every kind of photo, because the pattern is hard to pick out.
It gives mostly correct answers, even though it learned from a small set.

feedback.correct: Well matched - an error teaches a false pattern, a gap leaves a whole case unseen, noise blurs the pattern everywhere, and a small clean set can still do well.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each flaw teaches the model: a wrong label teaches a wrong thing, a missing kind of date cannot be learned at all, and noise makes every case harder.

g6-bridging-w1-core.prompt: Put these four steps in order to trace how one problem in the data becomes one wrong answer.

items.text: A photo of a stone is put into the dataset with the label "date".
The model studies the dataset and adjusts itself to match the patterns it finds.
The model now treats small round grey objects as dates.
Shown a new photo of a pebble, the model answers "date".

feedback.correct: That is the causal chain: a problem in the data, then a pattern learned from it, then the wrong output it produces.
feedback.incorrect: Start at the data, not the answer - the flawed example comes first, the model learns from it, and only then does the wrong output appear.

g6-bridging-w1-core.prompt: A team re-photographs every blurry item so it is sharp, and rewrites the labels that had been spelled three different ways. The dataset still holds exactly the same photos of exactly the same dates - none are added and none are taken away. Based on the lesson, the AI’s outputs should get better.

feedback.correct: Yes - taking out noise makes the pattern easier to learn, and that is a quality improvement even though the dataset is exactly the same size.
feedback.incorrect: The amount of data did not change, but the noise did: less blur and consistent labels make the pattern clearer, so the outputs should improve.

g6-bridging-w1-lab.prompt:
A team ran the same task with the same model on four versions of one dataset, and scored each against the clean baseline.

Version A (clean set): 19 of 20 correct.
Version B (blurry photos, labels spelled three ways): 14 of 20 correct, and many answers were unsure.
Version C (no yellow dates in the set): 11 of 20 correct - every yellow date wrong, the rest right.
Version D (some stones labelled "date"): 7 of 20 correct, and it repeated wrong labels confidently.

Rank the four versions by how many of the 20 items each one got right, best first.

items.text: Version B - blurry photos and labels spelled three ways
Version D - some stones labelled "date"
Version A - the clean set
Version C - no yellow dates in the set

feedback.correct: That is a ranking built on evidence: the order follows what the outputs actually did, from 19 of 20 correct down to 7 of 20 with confident wrong labels.
feedback.incorrect: Rank by what each version's output did, not by how bad the flaw sounds - match each version back to its recorded score before placing it on the line.

g6-bridging-w1-lab.prompt: The team wants their investigation to show that the differences in the outputs really came from the data. Which plan makes it a fair test?

options.text: Keep the task and the model the same for every version, and change only the dataset.
Give each dataset a different model, so every dataset gets its best chance.
Change the dataset and make the task harder at the same time, so the differences are easier to see.
Test each dataset on a different task, then compare the average scores.

feedback.correct: Exactly - when only the dataset changes, any difference in the output can be traced back to the data, and that is what makes your evidence trustworthy.
feedback.incorrect: If more than one thing changes between versions, you can no longer tell whether the data or the other change caused the difference.

g6-bridging-w1-lab.prompt: A ranking has to be justified with evidence from the outputs, not opinion. Select every line below that counts as evidence.

options.text: The error version called 3 of the 5 stones "date"; the clean version called none of them dates.
The noisy version got 14 of 20 right - six fewer than the clean baseline.
The gap version got every yellow date wrong, while the baseline got all of them right.
Our team all agreed that the noisy dataset felt like the worst one.
The error version must be worst, because wrong data is always the worst thing.

feedback.correct: Yes - evidence is a specific observation of what the output did, and each of those points to an exact change you could show someone.
feedback.incorrect: Agreeing as a team or stating a general rule is not evidence; evidence names the exact output change, such as how many items shifted from right to wrong.

g6-bridging-w1-lab.prompt: Match each change the team saw in the output to the data flaw responsible for it.

left.text: It gives a wrong name to certain items, and repeats the same wrong name confidently every time.
It gets every example of one whole category wrong, but handles the other categories well.
Its answers are unsure and inconsistent across every kind of item, with no one category failing more than the rest.
Its answers stay close to the baseline on every kind of item.

right.text: Wrong labels in the training data (an error)
A missing category in the training data (a gap)
Blurry photos and labels spelled three different ways (noise)
No flaw - this is the clean dataset

feedback.correct: Well matched - each flaw leaves its own fingerprint: an error is confident and repeated, a gap hits one category only, and noise spreads uncertainty everywhere.
feedback.incorrect: Look at where the damage lands: one category only points to a gap, confident repeated wrong names point to wrong labels, and uncertainty across everything points to noise.

g6-bridging-w1-lab.prompt: Complete this line from the team's investigation log: "We kept the task and the model the same and changed only the (1), and we compared every version against the clean result, which we call the (2)."
blanks: (1) the one thing they changed between versions
(2) the name for the clean result everything is compared against

feedback.correct: That is the whole method in one line: change only the dataset, and measure every version against the baseline so your evidence means something.
feedback.incorrect: Only one thing changes in a fair test - the dataset - and the clean result you compare everything against is the baseline.

g6-bridging-w3-core.prompt: Two date-sorting apps run exactly the same code. Shown the same photo of a brown date, one app answers 'ripe' and the other answers 'unripe'. What is the best explanation?
options: The two apps learned from different sets of example photos, so each one found a different pattern.
One app's code must contain a mistake, because identical code always has to give identical answers.
One app is guessing, because apps answer at random whenever a photo is hard to judge.
The apps were given the same examples, but one of them studied the photo for longer.

feedback.correct: Right - the code is only half of a solution; the examples it learned from decide the pattern, and the pattern decides the outcome.
feedback.incorrect: Identical code can still disagree: each app built its model from different examples, so each learned a different pattern and gives a different outcome.

g6-bridging-w3-core.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how the data ends up shaping the sorter's answer about a new date.
items: The model captures the pattern it keeps seeing across those examples.
Photos of dates, each labelled ripe or unripe, are collected as the data.
The sorter gives an outcome for a new date it has never seen.
The model studies the collected examples.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the data comes first, the pattern comes from the data, and the outcome comes from the pattern.
feedback.incorrect: The chain runs data first: examples are collected, the model studies them, it captures a pattern, and only then can it give an outcome for a new date.

g6-bridging-w3-core.prompt: A sorter learned from 200 photos of brown ripe dates and only 5 photos of green unripe dates. Select ALL the changes that would move its outcomes a lot.
options: Adding 60 photos of green unripe dates.
Adding 60 more photos of brown ripe dates.
Adding 60 photos of half-ripe yellow dates, a colour it has never been shown.
Removing 3 of the 200 brown ripe photos.
Running the same 200 brown ripe photos through the model a second time.

feedback.correct: Yes - the green and yellow batches fill gaps in categories the sorter barely had, and gaps are where the outcome moves most.
feedback.incorrect: Adding, removing or repeating brown photos only reinforces a pattern the sorter already has; it is the missing or rare categories, green and yellow, that shift the outcome.

g6-bridging-w3-core.prompt: True or false: for a sorter that already learned from 200 brown ripe dates, adding 100 more brown ripe photos will change its outcomes more than adding 20 green unripe photos would.

feedback.correct: Correct - size alone does not decide influence; 20 photos of a category the sorter is missing shift the outcome more than 100 more of what it already has.
feedback.incorrect: It is false: the 100 extra brown photos repeat a pattern the sorter already learned, while the 20 green photos fill a gap, and filling a gap moves the outcome far more.

g6-bridging-w3-core.prompt: The sorter learned from 200 brown ripe dates and 5 green unripe dates. Match each change to the outcome you should predict from it.
left: Add 50 photos of green dates labelled 'unripe'.
Add 50 more photos of brown dates labelled 'ripe'.
Change nothing in the data, but let a different class use the app.
right: The sorter starts calling green dates 'unripe' - a big shift, because a missing category has been filled.
The outcome barely moves, because the new examples repeat a pattern the sorter already had plenty of.
The outcome stays exactly the same, because it comes from the data and the model, not from who is using the app.

feedback.correct: Well matched - you predicted each outcome from what the data gained, which is exactly how a data detective reasons.
feedback.incorrect: Predict from the gap: new examples of a missing category move the outcome, more of the same barely does, and changing the user changes nothing at all.

g6-bridging-w3-lab.prompt: A group swapped in the green-date batch AND the yellow-date batch at the same time. The sorter's answer changed from 'ripe' to 'unripe'. What should they write in their log?
options: We cannot tell which batch moved the outcome, so we will redo the test changing one batch at a time.
Both batches are equally influential, because the outcome moved when we swapped them together.
The larger batch caused the change, because a bigger batch always has the bigger effect.
The test worked fine - swapping two batches at once saves time and gives us the same evidence.

feedback.correct: Right - with two changes at once the result cannot be attributed to either batch, so the fair test has to be run again one batch at a time.
feedback.incorrect: When two batches change together the shift could have come from either one, or from both; only a single controlled swap tells you which batch did it.

g6-bridging-w3-lab.prompt: Put the steps of one fair data-swap test into the order you should carry them out.
items: Swap in one data batch, and only that batch.
Record the outcome for your test fruit before you change anything.
Re-run the winning swap on a fresh fruit to check the effect repeats.
Compare the two recorded outcomes and write down the size of the shift.
Record the outcome for the same test fruit again.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the 'before' has to be recorded first, or there is nothing to compare the 'after' with, and verifying comes last.
feedback.incorrect: A fair test records the before outcome first, changes one batch, records the after outcome, measures the shift, and only then verifies the winner on a fresh fruit.

g6-bridging-w3-lab.prompt: Three rows from an investigation log on a sorter trained mostly on brown ripe dates. Match each row to what the evidence in it shows.
left: Added 40 more brown ripe photos. Before: 'ripe'. After: 'ripe'.
Added 40 green unripe photos. Before (green date): 'ripe'. After: 'unripe'.
Kept the 40 green unripe photos and tested a second, fresh green date. Before: 'ripe'. After: 'unripe'.
right: No influence - the batch repeated a pattern the sorter already had plenty of, so nothing shifted.
Influential - the batch filled a gap in the data and the outcome changed.
Verified - the same change moved the outcome again on a fresh fruit, so the effect is real, not a one-off.

feedback.correct: Well read - a row with no shift shows no influence, a row with a shift shows influence, and a repeat of that shift on a fresh fruit is verification.
feedback.incorrect: Read each row's before and after: no movement means no influence, movement means influence, and the same movement repeating on a fresh fruit is what verifies it.

g6-bridging-w3-lab.prompt: True or false: once a swap has moved the outcome one time, that single result is enough proof that the batch is the most influential one - there is no need to test it again.

feedback.correct: Correct - one result could be a coincidence, so you re-run the swap on a fresh fruit to verify the effect repeats.
feedback.incorrect: It is false: a single moved outcome might be a one-off, so you verify by re-running the swap on a fresh fruit and checking the effect happens again.

g6-bridging-w3-lab.prompt: Your log shows Swap A: no shift, Swap B: a big shift, Swap C: a little shift, and a re-run of Swap B on a fresh date that shifted the same way. Select ALL the conclusions your evidence actually supports.
options: Of the three swaps we tested, Swap B was the most influential, because our log shows it produced the biggest before/after shift.
Swap B's effect is real and not a coincidence, because the re-run on a fresh date moved the outcome the same way.
Swap B is the most influential data change that exists for any sorter anywhere.
Swap A and Swap C can never change the outcome of any solution.
Swap B must be the winner because it is the one we predicted would win before we started.

feedback.correct: Yes - your conclusions stay inside what you actually recorded: the biggest logged shift, confirmed by a repeat run.
feedback.incorrect: A conclusion must not go further than the log: you tested three swaps on one sorter, and a prediction you made beforehand is not evidence - the recorded shifts are.

g6-bridging-w4-core.prompt: An AI answer reads: "The festival opened in 2007 and drew 41,000 visitors on its first day." Your group has to name the misinformation risk. Which statement names the risk in the way this lesson asks for?

options.text: The answer is probably wrong somewhere, because AI is not always right.
The date 2007 and the figure 41,000 could be invented, because the system predicts words that sound likely instead of looking facts up.
The answer is written with no hedging, so the facts inside it are most likely correct.
There is no risk to name, because the sentence is clear and easy to read.

feedback.correct: Pointing at the exact date and number tells you precisely what to check, which "it might be wrong" never does.
feedback.incorrect: Name the exact claim you doubt - the number, date, name or source - because a general worry gives you nothing to verify.

g6-bridging-w4-core.prompt: Match each doubtful claim from an AI output to the check that would actually settle it.

left.text: "The city's population passed four million last year."
"This poem was written by the poet Al Khansa."
"The museum stays open until 8pm on Fridays."
"A 2021 study found that pupils who sleep more score higher."

right.text: Look the figure up in the official population statistics published for that year.
Search a library catalogue for the poem's title and see who it is credited to.
Read the opening-hours page on the museum's own website.
Find the study itself and read whether it exists and says that.
Ask the AI whether it is sure, and accept the claim if it repeats it.
Ask a friend whether the claim sounds about right to them.

feedback.correct: A check only works if it targets the exact claim and comes from a source that is independent of the AI.
feedback.incorrect: Match the claim to the source that holds that kind of fact - and remember the AI repeating itself, or a friend's hunch, is not a trusted source.

g6-bridging-w4-core.prompt: An AI answer that is fluent and sounds confident is good evidence that the facts inside it are correct.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the system is built to sound plausible, so an invented number reads exactly like a real one.
feedback.incorrect: Fluency is about how the words are chosen, not whether they are true; confident writing can still carry a made-up figure.

g6-bridging-w4-core.prompt: Sara has checked an AI claim about a record-breaking building against one official website. She is deciding whether to add a second, independent trusted source. Which of these are good reasons to add one? Select all that apply.

options.text: One source can be out of date, and a second source would reveal that.
Two sources that do not copy each other are unlikely to carry the same mistake.
Asking the AI again and getting the same answer counts as a second source.
A second source makes the claim certain, so no doubt is left at all.
A check that takes longer is automatically a better check.

feedback.correct: Layering helps because the second source can fail separately from the first - that is what independence means.
feedback.incorrect: A second source earns its place only by being independent; repeating the AI, or simply taking longer, adds no new evidence, and even two sources raise confidence rather than give certainty.

g6-bridging-w4-core.prompt: Complete the rule this lesson gives: an AI system is built to sound ___ rather than to be ___, so before you share a claim you should check it against a trusted source that is ___ of the AI.

feedback.correct: That is the whole habit in one sentence: plausible is not true, so verify against something the AI did not produce.
feedback.incorrect: The system aims at plausible rather than true, which is why the check has to come from a source independent of the AI.

g6-bridging-w4-lab.prompt: Your group is handed a new suspect output. Put the four steps of the verification routine in the order the lesson uses.

items.text: Isolate the exact claim the output is making.
Pick a trusted source that is independent of the AI.
Compare the claim with what that source says.
Record the verdict: verified, false or unclear.

feedback.correct: Running the same fixed steps on every output is what stops a slick answer getting an easy pass.
feedback.incorrect: The routine gathers evidence before it judges: isolate the claim, choose an independent source, compare, and only then record the verdict.

g6-bridging-w4-lab.prompt: Your group has run the routine on four outputs. Match what the source-checker found to the verdict the recorder should write.

left.text: The official site gives the same tower height as the output.
The official site gives a different opening date from the output.
No trusted source on the reference sheet mentions the claim at all.
Two sites agree, but the second says its figures were taken from the first.

right.text: Verified - an independent trusted source agrees with the claim.
False - a trusted source contradicts the claim.
Unclear - no source covers it, so there is no evidence either way.
Count it as one source - they are not independent, so they could share the same error.
Verified - the output sounded confident and nothing has contradicted it.

feedback.correct: Every verdict is tied to what the evidence showed - including the honest 'unclear' and the copied source that only looks like two.
feedback.incorrect: A verdict reports what the trusted source showed: agreement, contradiction, no evidence at all, or sources that copy each other and therefore count as one.

g6-bridging-w4-lab.prompt: Your group checks the claim "the festival first ran in 1998". None of the trusted sources on the reference sheet mention the festival's first year. What should the verdict-recorder write, and why?

options.text: Verified - nothing contradicted the claim, so it stands.
False - if a trusted source does not mention it, the claim must be made up.
Unclear - no trusted source covers this claim, so there is no evidence either way.
Verified - the output gave the year with no hesitation, and confident claims are usually right.

feedback.correct: 'Unclear' is an honest verdict: it records that the evidence is missing instead of inventing a judgement.
feedback.incorrect: Missing evidence is not proof that a claim is false, and it is not permission to pass it either - the routine lets you record 'unclear'.

g6-bridging-w4-lab.prompt: Your group has ten outputs and limited time, so you will only cross-check some of them with a second source. Which of these are sound reasons for spending the extra time on a particular output? Select all that apply.

options.text: Getting this claim wrong would matter to the people who read it, so confidence is worth more than speed here.
The one source you used could be out of date, so a single check might miss an error.
The output sounds confident and polished, so it needs less checking than the others.
The second source you would add is run by the same organisation as the first.
Your group has spare time, and spare time is what makes a check reliable.

feedback.correct: You spend the extra time where a wrong verdict would cost most, or where one source could quietly be wrong.
feedback.incorrect: Choose by what is at stake and by how the first source could fail - not by how confident the output sounds, and not by adding a source that would fail alongside the first.

g6-bridging-w4-lab.prompt: Complete the trade-off from the lab: a single-source check is ___, but your verdict is wrong if that one source is wrong; a two-source cross-check is ___, yet much harder to fool because the two sources are ___ of each other.
blanks: the two sources are ___ of each other

feedback.correct: That is the judgement in one line: you trade speed for confidence, and the confidence comes from independence.
feedback.incorrect: The cross-check costs time and buys reliability - two sources that do not copy each other rarely make the same mistake.

g6-bridging-w5-core.prompt: Layla's helper has one task: recommend a library book for her class. She has the class reading survey as her data. Which of these is the best structured prompt for that task?

options.text: Suggest a good book.
Using our class reading survey, suggest one book most of the class would enjoy, and give one sentence saying why.
Using our class reading survey, suggest some books people might like.
Suggest one book and write as much as you possibly can about it, in as much detail as you can manage.

feedback.correct: That prompt gives the goal, the details (which data to use) and the form of the answer, so the helper knows exactly what to produce.
feedback.incorrect: A structured prompt needs all three: the goal, the details such as which data to use, and the form the answer should take - being longer or politer is not the same as being structured.

g6-bridging-w5-core.prompt: Layla's finished helper is described below. Match each part of her description to the part of the helper it is.

left.text: Recommend one library book that most of the class would enjoy
The 28 completed class reading surveys
Using the class reading survey, name one book and give one sentence saying why
'The Lost Ship' - because 19 pupils chose adventure stories

right.text: The task
The data
The structured prompt
The output

feedback.correct: A helper is a task, a structured prompt and data - and what comes back out of it is the output, not one of its parts.
feedback.incorrect: The task is the job to be done, the data is what the helper reads, the structured prompt is the instruction you write, and the output is what the helper gives back.

g6-bridging-w5-core.prompt: Sami's survey data has several entries typed in twice and a few answers copied into the wrong column. He rewrites his prompt so it is very precise. True or false: the precise prompt will make up for the messy data, so the output can be trusted.

feedback.correct: Right - the output is built from the data as well as the prompt, so poor data still gives a poor output however precise the wording is.
feedback.incorrect: A prompt only tells the helper what to do with the data it is given; if the data is wrong, a better-worded instruction cannot invent the right answer.

g6-bridging-w5-core.prompt: Put the steps of a clean-versus-noisy data test in the order you would carry them out.

items.text: Write the task your helper must do.
Write the structured prompt and prepare the clean data.
Run the helper on the clean data and note the output.
Run the same prompt on the noisy version of the data and note the output.
Compare the two outputs and explain how the data quality caused the difference.

feedback.correct: Keeping the prompt the same and changing only the data is what makes the difference in the outputs fair to blame on data quality.
feedback.incorrect: Design first, then run the clean data, then run the very same prompt on the noisy data - only then can you compare and explain the difference.

g6-bridging-w5-core.prompt: Kareem's helper recommends whichever genre the most survey responses chose. His clean survey has 20 responses: 11 chose adventure and 9 chose sport. By mistake, some of the sport responses are copied and counted again. What is the smallest number of copied sport responses that would make the helper recommend sport instead of adventure?

feedback.correct: Three copies take sport from 9 to 12, just past adventure's 11 - a handful of duplicated rows is enough to flip the recommendation.
feedback.incorrect: Sport needs more than adventure's 11, and two copies only make it 11, which is a tie - so it takes three copies to overturn the real result.

g6-bridging-w5-lab.prompt: Sam's prompt v1 is 'Suggest a book.' The output was a vague list. He wants his v2 to show him what actually helped. Which v2 is the best next step?

options.text: Using our class reading survey, suggest a book.
Using our class reading survey, suggest one book, give one sentence saying why, and keep it friendly.
Please could you kindly suggest a book for us? Thank you very much!
Suggest a film instead.

feedback.correct: Only one part of the prompt changed, so any improvement in the output can be pinned on naming the data.
feedback.incorrect: Changing several parts at once hides which one helped, extra politeness adds words but no precision, and changing the task means you are no longer testing the same helper.

g6-bridging-w5-lab.prompt: Match each change Sam made to his prompt with the effect you would expect it to have on the output.

left.text: Added 'using our class reading survey'
Added 'name one book, not a list'
Added 'give one sentence saying why'
Added 'please be as helpful and friendly as you can'

right.text: The answer is now based on the class's own data instead of a general guess.
The answer is a single choice instead of several.
The answer now explains the reason behind the choice.
The prompt got longer, but the answer is no more useful.

feedback.correct: Each useful change targets one thing - the data, the number of answers, or the reasoning - while extra friendly words only make the prompt longer.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each change tells the helper to do differently; a change that adds no new instruction changes the length of the prompt, not the quality of the output.

g6-bridging-w5-lab.prompt: Maya claims her v3 is better than her v2, and that her change is what made it better. Which of these count as good evidence for her claim? Select all that apply.

options.text: v3's output names one book, which is what her task asked for.
v3's prompt has more words in it than v2's.
v3's output gives a reason, so Maya can judge whether the choice makes sense.
Only one part of the prompt changed between v2 and v3, so Maya knows what caused the change.
v3's prompt sounds more polite than v2's.

feedback.correct: Better means the output meets the task and can be judged, and a single change is what lets Maya say which edit caused it.
feedback.incorrect: A longer or politer prompt is not evidence of a better output - the evidence is that the output now meets the task, can be judged, and followed one change you can point to.

g6-bridging-w5-lab.prompt: Omar changes three parts of his prompt at the same time and the output gets much better. True or false: he can still say which of the three changes caused the improvement.

feedback.correct: Right - with three edits made together any of them, or all of them, could be responsible, so he would have to test them one at a time.
feedback.incorrect: A better output only tells you the new prompt as a whole works better; to name the change that helped, you have to change one part at a time.

g6-bridging-w5-lab.prompt: Sam's log: v2 'Using our class reading survey, suggest a book' returned a list with no explanation. v3 'Using our class reading survey, suggest one book and give one sentence saying why' returned a single title with a reason. Complete the explanation: the change from v2 to v3 improved the output because it told the helper to name ___ book and to give a ___.

feedback.correct: Naming how many answers and asking for the thinking behind them is what turned a vague list into something the class can judge.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the two prompts word by word: v3 asks for one book rather than several, and asks the helper to say why it chose it.

g6-bridging-w6-core.prompt: Maya's helper suggests one book for her class. It uses the class survey, in which 9 of the 20 pupils picked adventure and only 4 picked science. Maya then adds 12 more replies from the science club, and every one of them picks science. She runs the helper again on the new data. What is the best prediction of what happens to the suggestion?
options: It is likely to change to a science book, because science is now the most-picked genre in the data.
It stays an adventure book, because the helper already chose adventure the first time.
It stays an adventure book, because only a new prompt can change what the helper suggests.
It becomes unpredictable, because the helper now has replies from two different groups.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the suggestion follows the data, so once science becomes the most-picked genre the suggestion moves with it.
feedback.incorrect: The helper does not remember its earlier answer and does not need a new prompt; it counts the data it is given again, and science (16) now beats adventure (9).

g6-bridging-w6-core.prompt: Ben's helper claims that adventure was the most popular genre in his class. Ben asks the same helper the same question again, gets the same answer, and writes on his plan that the claim is verified. Ben has verified his claim.

feedback.correct: Right - asking the same tool twice only repeats it; verifying means checking the claim against a trusted source outside the tool, such as the survey totals themselves.
feedback.incorrect: A tool that is wrong once will usually be wrong the same way twice, so repeating the question proves nothing - verification means checking the claim against a trusted, independent source.

g6-bridging-w6-core.prompt: Each row on the left is a risk a pupil found in their helper. Match each risk to the mitigation that would reduce it.
left: One pupil's reply was entered twice, so that pupil's opinion is counted double.
The output names a pupil and says which class they are in.
Only the pupils in the chess club answered the survey, so most of the class is missing.
The helper states a fact about the class that nobody has checked.
right: Check the fact against the survey totals before using it.
Delete the repeated reply so that each pupil counts once.
Take the personal details out so that the output names nobody.
Collect replies from the rest of the class before running the helper again.

feedback.correct: Well matched - a mitigation has to fix the particular thing that could go wrong, not just be a generally sensible action.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each risk would do to the output: a double-counted reply needs the duplicate removed, a named pupil needs the personal details taken out, a missing group needs more replies, and an unchecked fact needs verifying.

g6-bridging-w6-core.prompt: Trace how the data leads to the outcome in Maya's book helper. Put these four steps into the order in which they happen.
items: The helper suggests an adventure book to the class.
Every pupil's genre choice is collected in the class survey.
Adventure comes out as the most-picked genre.
The helper counts how many pupils picked each genre.

feedback.correct: That is the trace: data first, then the counting, then the result, and the result drives the suggestion - which is why changing the data changes the outcome.
feedback.incorrect: Follow the data forwards: the replies are collected, then counted, the count gives the top genre, and only then does the helper suggest a book.

g6-bridging-w6-core.prompt: Which of these belong in a good check plan for an AI helper? Choose all that apply.
options: Compare the helper's claim with the survey totals yourself.
Ask the same helper the question again and accept the answer if it matches the first one.
Look for a reply that was entered twice and remove it before trusting the result.
Check whether the output includes details that could identify a pupil, and take them out.
Ask the helper to say its answer more confidently so that it sounds more reliable.

feedback.correct: Yes - a real check plan compares the output with something trustworthy outside the tool and looks for ways the output could be wrong or unfair.
feedback.incorrect: Repeating the question and making the wording sound more confident change nothing about whether the answer is true; the checks that count compare the claim with a trusted source and hunt for risks in the data and the output.

g6-bridging-w6-lab.prompt: Sam's helper says 'most of our class picked adventure'. He checks the class survey totals: adventure 7, science 11. His verification has failed. What should he do next?
options: Refine the helper so that its claim fits the data, then verify the claim again.
Keep the output as it is and add a note saying that it might be wrong.
Ask the helper the same question again and use whichever answer it gives.
Change the survey totals so that they agree with the helper's claim.

feedback.correct: Exactly - a failed check is useful information: you refine the helper and then re-verify, rather than keeping an output you know does not match the data.
feedback.incorrect: A failed check means the output is wrong, so warning labels, re-asking the tool, or editing the real totals all leave the mistake in place - refine the helper, then verify again.

g6-bridging-w6-lab.prompt: Sam's first verification failed. Put these five steps into the order he should follow to fix his helper and show that it can be trusted.
items: He checks the new claim against the survey totals again, and this time it matches.
He checks the helper's claim against the class survey totals.
He uses the passed check as evidence that his helper can be trusted.
He finds that the claim does not match the totals.
He changes the helper so that its claim follows the data.

feedback.correct: That is the verify-refine-re-verify loop: you can only argue that a helper is trustworthy after a check has actually been passed.
feedback.incorrect: Check first, and only then find the problem, change the helper, and check again - the trust argument comes last, because it rests on the check that finally passed.

g6-bridging-w6-lab.prompt: Which of these count as evidence that a helper can be trusted? Choose all that apply.
options: I checked the claim 'adventure was picked most' against the survey totals, and it matched.
I removed the duplicate reply, ran the helper again, and now no pupil is counted twice.
The helper answered very quickly and never hesitated.
I asked the helper whether it was sure, and it said yes.
I took the pupils' names out of the output and checked that none were left.

feedback.correct: Yes - evidence is a check you actually carried out and the result it gave, not how confident or fast the helper seemed.
feedback.incorrect: Speed and a confident 'yes' from the tool tell you nothing about whether the output is right; evidence is a check you carried out against something trustworthy, and a mitigation you applied and then re-checked.

g6-bridging-w6-lab.prompt: In your reflection you look back across the four skills you used. Match each skill to the piece of work that shows it.
left: Data quality
Prompt refinement
Data influence
Verification and risk
right: I showed that the most-picked genre in the survey is what decided the suggestion.
I found two replies from the same pupil and removed one before using the data.
I checked the claim against the survey totals and took the pupils' names out of the output.
My first instruction gave a vague answer, so I rewrote it to ask for one book and a reason.

feedback.correct: Well matched - each skill leaves a different trace in your work, which is what makes a reflection specific rather than vague.
feedback.incorrect: Cleaning the data is data quality, rewriting the instruction is prompt refinement, showing which data decided the output is data influence, and checking a claim or reducing a risk is verification and risk.

g6-bridging-w6-lab.prompt: Leila's helper suggests one book for the whole class, and all of her checks passed. A friend now wants to use the same helper to label which pupils are 'good readers' and which are not. Which rule best fits what this lesson teaches about risk?
options: Use the helper to suggest a book for the class, but not to label individual pupils, because a wrong or unfair output would judge a real person.
Use it for both, as long as you tell people that an AI made the decision.
Use it for both, because the data behind the helper has already been checked once.
Stop using the helper altogether, because any output it gives could turn out to be wrong.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the same helper carries a much bigger risk when its output labels a person, so the sensible rule limits it to the use where a mistake is easy to spot and easy to undo.
feedback.incorrect: Passing checks for one job does not make a helper safe for every job - announcing that an AI decided, or checking the data once, does not undo the harm of unfairly labelling a pupil, and the book suggestion was already shown to be trustworthy.

g6-main-w1-core.prompt: A spam filter was built by showing a computer thousands of emails that people had already labelled 'spam' or 'not spam'. Nobody wrote a rule for every email. Which sorting and reason is correct?
options: Learns from data, because it found the pattern itself from many labelled example emails.
Follows fixed rules, because a person had to label the example emails first.
Learns from data, because it gets faster the more emails you send it.
Follows fixed rules, because a person wrote a step for every kind of email it might meet.
g6-main-w1-core.answer: Learns from data, because it found the pattern itself from many labelled example emails.

feedback.correct: Right - the logic came from the examples, not from steps a person wrote, which is exactly what makes it a learning system.
feedback.incorrect: People labelled the examples, but nobody wrote a rule for each email - the filter found the pattern in that data itself, so it learns from data.

g6-main-w1-core.prompt: A photo app was shown 10,000 photos that people had already labelled 'cat' or 'not cat', and it worked out the pattern for itself. A Salik toll gate charges every car that passes, because a person wrote that step. Match each part of the story to the word that names it.
left: The 10,000 labelled photos the app was shown
One single labelled photo out of that collection
The pattern the app built so it can spot cats in photos it has never seen
The toll gate, which charges every car because a person wrote that step
right: data
example
model
rule-based system

feedback.correct: Good - you used the words on a real case: many examples make up the data, the pattern built from them is the model, and written steps make a rule-based system.
feedback.incorrect: The whole collection shown to the app is the data, one photo from it is an example, the pattern built from them is the model, and the toll gate with its written step is the rule-based system.

g6-main-w1-core.prompt: You want to work out whether a new app follows fixed rules or learns from data. Which questions would actually help you decide? Choose all that would help.
options: Was it shown lots of examples that people had already labelled?
Did a person write a step for every case the app has to handle?
Would the app behave differently if it had been shown different examples?
How quickly does the app give you an answer?
Which company made the app, and how new is it?
answer: Was it shown lots of examples that people had already labelled?
Did a person write a step for every case the app has to handle?
Would the app behave differently if it had been shown different examples?

feedback.correct: Yes - good questions go after where the logic came from: written steps, or a pattern found in examples.
feedback.incorrect: Speed and who made it are the same for both kinds. The useful questions ask where the logic came from - written steps, or examples the app learned a pattern from.

g6-main-w1-core.prompt: True or false? A learning system is really just a very long list of fixed rules that a programmer typed in, one rule for every case.

feedback.correct: Correct - no one types a rule for every case; the system is shown many examples and builds the pattern itself.
feedback.incorrect: That is the common mix-up. A learning system has no written rule for each case - it finds the pattern from the examples it is shown.

g6-main-w1-core.prompt: Fill in each gap with either 'follows fixed rules' or 'learns from data'. A toll gate charges every car as it passes, because a person wrote that step for it, so it ___(1). A spam filter was shown thousands of emails already labelled spam or not spam and worked out the pattern itself, so it ___(2).

feedback.correct: Well sorted - you used the deciding clue each time: who supplied the logic, a person or the examples.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who supplied the logic. A person wrote the toll gate's step, so it follows fixed rules; the filter found its own pattern in the examples, so it learns from data.

g6-main-w1-lab.prompt: Sam is given a mystery machine and wants to find out whether it follows fixed rules or learns. Which test would actually tell him?
options: Give it a brand-new, unusual input and watch whether it reacts the same as always or tries to match a pattern.
Give it only inputs it has handled before and check that the answers are still right.
Give it the same easy input five times and time how fast each answer comes back.
Count how many different answers the machine can give altogether.
g6-main-w1-lab.answer: Give it a brand-new, unusual input and watch whether it reacts the same as always or tries to match a pattern.

feedback.correct: Exactly - a new, unusual input is what splits them: fixed rules react the same or break, while a learning system reaches for the pattern it built.
feedback.incorrect: Familiar inputs, speed and the number of answers look much the same for both kinds. Only a brand-new, unusual input shows whether the machine follows a written step or matches a pattern.

g6-main-w1-lab.prompt: Put these steps in order to run a fair test on a mystery machine.
items: Write down the unusual input you will try and what each possible result would mean.
Give that unusual input to the machine.
Record exactly what the machine did.
Use what you recorded to decide whether the machine follows fixed rules or learns.

feedback.correct: That is how a detective works - decide what each result would mean before you test, so the result can't be bent to fit afterwards.
feedback.incorrect: Plan first: write the input and what each result would mean, then test, then record what happened, and only then decide which kind of machine it is.

g6-main-w1-lab.prompt: Match each thing a group tried at the two stations with what happened.
left: Fed the rule-card machine the same card twice
Fed the rule-card machine a strange card that no rule covered
Gave the card game example cards that were all of one kind
Gave the card game plenty of varied, correctly labelled example cards
right: It gave exactly the same output both times.
It stopped, because no step had been written for that card.
The pattern it built came out lopsided and it sorted new cards badly.
The pattern it built sorted most of the new cards correctly.

feedback.correct: Good - each machine fails in its own way: fixed rules break on a case with no rule, and a learning system is only as good as the examples it was shown.
feedback.incorrect: The rule-card machine repeats itself and breaks when no rule fits; the card game's guesses follow the examples it was given, so one-sided examples make a lopsided pattern.

g6-main-w1-lab.prompt: True or false? A rule-based machine can still fail: if it meets an input that none of its rules covers, it stops or gives a wrong answer.

feedback.correct: Yes - following fixed rules does not mean never failing; it means failing whenever something turns up that has no rule.
feedback.incorrect: Fixed rules are predictable, not perfect. At Station A the strange card had no rule, so the machine stopped or answered wrongly.

g6-main-w1-lab.prompt: Fill in the gaps. We tested a mystery machine with a brand-new, unusual input, and it gave exactly the answer it always gives, so we decided it ___(1). The Station B card game behaved differently: it tried to match the ___(2) it had built from the example cards.

feedback.correct: That is the difference in one sentence: fixed rules repeat themselves, while a learning system reaches for the pattern it built from its examples.
feedback.incorrect: An unchanged answer to a brand-new input points to fixed rules; the card game instead matched the pattern it had built from the example cards.

g6-main-w2-core.prompt: A metro ticket gate opens only when a valid card is tapped. An engineer wrote out every condition the gate checks before it opens. Which classification and reason is correct?

options.text: Rule-based, because a person wrote the logic the gate follows.
Learning, because it builds a model from the thousands of cards tapped each day.
Rule-based, because the gate is simple and does not have a modern screen.
Learning, because it deals with a new passenger it has never seen before.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the deciding feature is where the logic came from, and here a person wrote it as fixed steps.
feedback.incorrect: Handling lots of taps, or looking plain, are surface traits; what decides it is that a person wrote the conditions rather than the system finding them in data.

g6-main-w2-core.prompt: Each clue below is evidence about a system. Match each clue to what it proves about that system.

left.text: You can open the file and read every step the machine follows, written out by its maker.
The system was shown thousands of labelled examples before it worked at all.
It refuses any case its maker did not write a step for.
It handled a phrase correctly that nobody had ever typed into it before.

right.text: Rule-based: the logic came from a person.
Learning: the logic came from data.
Rule-based: it only handles cases its rules cover.
Learning: it handles new cases that look like its examples.

feedback.correct: You used both features: where the logic came from, and what happens when something new arrives.
feedback.incorrect: Two clues are about where the logic came from and two are about what happens with a new case - sort them by which feature each one is really telling you about.

g6-main-w2-core.prompt: Select every piece of evidence that would be good proof that a system is a learning system.

options.text: It was shown labelled examples before it could do the job.
It gets new cases right that look like its examples.
Changing the examples it was shown changes the answers it gives.
Its screen is colourful and it updates every month.
It gives its answer almost instantly.
A person wrote out every step it follows.

feedback.correct: All three are about data building the logic - that is real proof, unlike how the system looks or how fast it is.
feedback.incorrect: Speed and a modern look are surface traits, and a person writing every step is proof of the opposite; pick the clues that point to data building the logic.

g6-main-w2-core.prompt: True or false: because a shopping app looks modern and changes its layout often, we can be sure it is a learning system.

feedback.correct: Right - looking modern is a surface trait, and a rule-based system can be given a shiny new layout at any time.
feedback.incorrect: A new look tells you nothing about where the logic came from; you would need evidence that the system built its logic from examples.

g6-main-w2-core.prompt: A spellchecker flags a word only when that word is missing from a fixed list its makers typed in. Complete the classification sentence.
g6-main-w2-core.stem: This is a {{1}} system, because a {{2}} wrote the logic.

feedback.correct: A fixed list typed in by its makers is logic written by a person, so this is rule-based.
feedback.incorrect: Ask where the logic came from: nobody showed this spellchecker labelled examples - a person typed the list, so it is rule-based.

g6-main-w2-lab.prompt: Put the lab steps in the order that gives a fair test of the model.

items.text: Pick two categories of non-personal items.
Collect and label 8-10 examples of each category.
Hide 3 examples of each category so the model will never see them.
Train the model using the remaining examples only.
Run the hidden examples through the model and log the results.

feedback.correct: The testing examples have to be set aside before training, or the model has already seen them and the test proves nothing.
feedback.incorrect: Check where the hiding step sits: examples must be held back before training, otherwise you are testing the model on work it already memorised.

g6-main-w2-lab.prompt: A group trained a 'cup' classifier. Every cup in their training examples was white. When they tested a red cup that had been held back, the model said 'not a cup'. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The model learned 'white' as well as 'cup', because every training example shared that colour.
The model simply did not have enough training examples.
The red cup was a testing example, and models always get testing examples wrong.
The model memorised the red cup during training and got confused.

feedback.correct: When every example shares a feature, the model learns that feature too - this is the red-cup version of the red-apple problem.
feedback.incorrect: More examples of the same white cups would not help, and the red cup was never in training; the problem is that the training examples had no variety in colour.

g6-main-w2-lab.prompt: A group wants to find out whether their model really learned 'circle' or only memorised their pictures. Select every action that would help them find out.

options.text: Test it on circles that were held back and never used in training.
Include circles of different sizes and colours among the testing examples.
Write down the prediction for each example before running it through the model.
Test it again using the same pictures it was trained on.
Add more copies of the training pictures to the testing set.
Judge the model by how quickly it gives each answer.

feedback.correct: Unseen and varied examples, with your prediction written first, is what turns a test into real evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Anything the model has already seen will be answered correctly whether it learned or memorised, and speed says nothing about what it learned.

g6-main-w2-lab.prompt: True or false: a model that gets every training example right but fails almost every held-back example has learned its categories well.

feedback.correct: Correct - getting the training examples right only shows it memorised them; real learning shows up on examples it has never seen.
feedback.incorrect: Scoring well on the examples it was trained on is easy; because it fails the held-back examples, this model memorised rather than learned.

g6-main-w2-lab.prompt: Complete the lab's rules about safe data and a fair check.
g6-main-w2-lab.stem: Training examples must be non-{{1}}, which means no faces, voices or names. The examples you hide are called {{2}} data, and they are a fair check only because the model never saw them during {{3}}.

feedback.correct: Safe data and a clean split between training and testing are the two things that make your log trustworthy.
feedback.incorrect: The golden rule is non-personal examples only, and the held-back set is the testing data - it works as a check because it stayed out of training.

g6-main-w3-core.prompt: Maya's task: give Grade 6 students exactly three bullet points on our school's recycling rules. She typed the prompt 'Tell me about recycling.' The tool returned six long paragraphs about recycling around the world. Which single adjustment does the most to complete Maya's task?
options: Run the same prompt again, because the tool gives a different answer each time.
Add 'make it shorter' to the end of the prompt she already used.
Rewrite it as 'Summarise our school's recycling rules for Grade 6 students in exactly three bullet points.'
Paste the six paragraphs back in and ask the tool whether they are correct.

feedback.correct: That rewrite supplies the goal (summarise the rules), the context (our school, Grade 6) and the format (exactly three bullets), so the tool can actually complete the task.
feedback.incorrect: The output missed the task on goal, context and format at once, so the fix has to put all three in - shortening or re-running a vague prompt still leaves the tool guessing.

g6-main-w3-core.prompt: Omar is writing a prompt for a class task. Match each line he wrote to the part of a structured prompt it belongs to.
left: Write a packing list for our Grade 6 desert field trip.
The trip is one day in February and we walk for two hours in the sun.
Give it as a numbered list of eight items, each under six words.
I am Omar Al Hosani, Class 6B, phone 050 ...
right: Goal - what you want the tool to do
Context - the details the tool needs
Format - how the answer should look
Leave this out - personal data never goes in a prompt

feedback.correct: Goal, context and format each do a different job, and personal details do none of them - they only put you at risk.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each line is for: the goal names the task, the context gives the tool the facts it needs, the format shapes the answer, and a name or phone number belongs in none of them.

g6-main-w3-core.prompt: Put the steps of today's task in the order the lesson used them.
items: Write down exactly what 'complete' would mean for this task.
Write the prompt with a goal, context and format.
Watch the prompt run on the approved tool.
Compare the output with the task and judge whether it was completed.
Change one thing in the prompt, run it again and verify the new output.

feedback.correct: Deciding what 'complete' means first is what lets you judge the output honestly and choose a useful adjustment afterwards.
feedback.incorrect: You cannot judge an output before you have decided what completing the task looks like, and the adjustment only makes sense after you have seen where the first output fell short.

g6-main-w3-core.prompt: True or false: if the output is long, well written and sounds confident, that is enough to show the task was completed.

feedback.correct: Right - you judge an output against what the task asked for, because a confident answer can still be incomplete or wrong.
feedback.incorrect: Sounding right is not the same as being right: check the output against the task you set, not against how polished it reads.

g6-main-w3-core.prompt: The task was: three bullet points on the water cycle for Grade 6, each under twelve words. The output came back with five bullets, two of them about twenty words long, and one bullet states something the science textbook says is wrong. Which of these show the task was NOT completed? Choose all that apply.
options: There are five bullets when the task asked for three.
Two of the bullets run to about twenty words.
One bullet is wrong when checked against the science textbook.
The answer is set out as bullet points instead of a paragraph.
The bullets are written in a friendly tone, which nobody asked for.

feedback.correct: Number, length and accuracy were all part of the task, so each of those three misses counts - and a wrong fact fails the task even when the format is perfect.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the output with the task line by line: bullets were requested and the tone was never specified, so only the count, the length and the wrong fact are genuine misses.

g6-main-w3-lab.prompt: The task had three requirements: name three school clubs, give the start time, and use a friendly tone. Structure A produced six lines that named three clubs, gave the start time and sounded friendly - but one club it named closed last year. Structure B produced twelve detailed lines, named two clubs, gave no start time and sounded friendly. Which judgement is the strongest?
options: Structure B is stronger because it gave far more detail than Structure A.
Structure A is stronger on completion, but its club list must be corrected after checking the school's club page.
Structure A is stronger, and because it met all three requirements there is nothing left to check.
Neither is stronger, because each output has a problem of some kind.

feedback.correct: You compared on completion and on accuracy: A met all three requirements, and the wrong club name is a fault to fix by verifying, not a reason to prefer the longer output.
feedback.incorrect: More words is not more complete, and meeting every requirement still does not prove the facts are right - judge completion first, then verify the winner against a reliable source.

g6-main-w3-lab.prompt: Which features make a prompt a reusable template rather than a one-off prompt? Choose all that apply.
options: It uses labelled slots such as 'Goal: [task]' that you fill in for each new task.
It ends with a step that checks the output against a reliable source.
It tells you to keep personal data out of the context.
It is longer and uses more words than a one-off prompt.
It names the exact topic of the first task you used it for.

feedback.correct: Slots let the template travel to new tasks, and the built-in verify and risk checks are what stop it being reused carelessly.
feedback.incorrect: A template is reusable because of its slots and its built-in checks - extra length adds nothing, and naming one task's topic locks the template to that task.

g6-main-w3-lab.prompt: Put the steps of the workshop in the order that lets you compare fairly and end with a template you can trust.
items: List the requirements the task has to meet.
Draft two prompts that use different structures.
Run both and mark which requirements each output met.
Check the facts in the stronger output against a reliable source.
Turn the stronger structure into a template with labelled slots and a verify step.

feedback.correct: The requirements come first because they are what you mark both structures against, and you only build a template out of a structure you have checked for accuracy.
feedback.incorrect: You need the requirements before you can say which structure completed more, and you should not turn a structure into a template until its output has survived an accuracy check.

g6-main-w3-lab.prompt: Complete the sentence about your template: A reusable template uses labelled ___ so the same skeleton fits many similar tasks, and it finishes with a step that tells you to ___ the output against a reliable source.

feedback.correct: Slots make the template reusable and the verify step makes it safe to reuse - a template without one is only half a template.
feedback.incorrect: A template needs both halves: labelled slots you fill in for each task, and a final instruction to verify the output against a reliable source.

g6-main-w3-lab.prompt: True or false: once your template has worked well on one task, you can use its output on a different task without checking it.

feedback.correct: Right - a template is a strong starting point, not a guarantee, so every new task still needs its output verified and risk-checked.
feedback.incorrect: A template that worked once only makes a good output more likely; the verify and risk steps are built in precisely because each new task can still go wrong.

g6-main-w4-core.prompt: Your task was: "Using the class fact sheet, write how long the River Nile is." The fact sheet on your desk says the Nile is 6,650 km long. The AI output says: "The River Nile is about 4,000 km long." Which verdict fits, and why?
options: Incorrect - it clashes with the length on the fact sheet, which you can check right now.
Unclear - the word "about" means the output is not giving an exact number.
Correct - it answers the task by giving a length in kilometres, as the task asked.
Unclear - you would need to find a second source before you could decide.

feedback.correct: Exactly - when an output clashes with a source you can check now, the verdict is incorrect, not unclear.
feedback.incorrect: You already have a source in front of you and 4,000 km clashes with its 6,650 km, so this is incorrect - 'unclear' is only for outputs you cannot check yet.

g6-main-w4-core.prompt: A reason must point to a check, not to a feeling. Select ALL the reasons below that are checkable reasons for a verdict.
options: The number in the output disagrees with the number on our fact sheet.
The output names "a recent study" but gives no title or date, so I cannot verify it.
The task asked for two examples and the output gives none.
It just feels wrong when I read it.
It is written confidently and has no spelling mistakes, so it must be right.

feedback.correct: Good - each of those points to something another person could check: a source, a missing detail, or the task itself.
feedback.incorrect: A checkable reason points to the task or to a source that someone else could look at; how an answer feels or how confident it sounds is not something anyone can check.

g6-main-w4-core.prompt: Match each output to the verdict it should be given.
left: The date in the output clashes with the date printed on the source card you were given.
The output does what the task asked and matches the trusted website you checked it against.
The output says "a recent study proved this" but gives no title, date or place you could look up.
right: Incorrect
Correct
Unclear

feedback.correct: That is the triage routine working: a clash means incorrect, a match with a trusted source means correct, and something you cannot check yet means unclear.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what you can check right now: a clash with a source is incorrect, a match is correct, and something with nothing to check against is unclear - not wrong, just not yet checkable.

g6-main-w4-core.prompt: True or false: an output that is written smoothly and sounds confident is more likely to be correct than one that is written awkwardly.

feedback.correct: Right - a language model predicts likely words, so confidence is a writing style and tells you nothing about whether the facts are true.
feedback.incorrect: Smooth, confident writing is just the style a language model produces; only a check against the task or a trusted source tells you whether it is right.

g6-main-w4-core.prompt: Put the five steps of the triage routine in the order you should carry them out.
items: Read the task the output was meant to answer.
Read the output carefully.
Check the output against the task and any source you were given.
Write your verdict: correct, incorrect, or unclear.
Add a short checkable reason and, if needed, one action.

feedback.correct: Yes - you read the task before the output, because you cannot judge an answer until you know what was asked, and the verdict only comes after the check.
feedback.incorrect: The task comes first (you cannot judge an answer without knowing what was asked), then the output, then the check - and only then do you write the verdict and its reason.

g6-main-w4-lab.prompt: At each clinic station, match the output to the verification action that fits it.
left: An output that states the Burj Khalifa is 828 m tall.
An output that summarises the article your group read at the station.
An output that says "follow the steps in the usual order" without listing any steps.
An output that says 4 tickets at 25 AED each cost 90 AED in total.
right: Look the height up in a trusted reference or official website.
Put it side by side with the original article and see whether it matches.
Write a clearer prompt asking for the steps to be listed one by one.
Work the calculation out yourself and compare the totals.

feedback.correct: Well matched - a claimed fact needs a trusted source, a summary needs the original text, a vague output needs a clearer prompt, and a calculation you can redo yourself.
feedback.incorrect: Match the check to the kind of output: facts go to a trusted source, summaries go back to the original text, vague outputs need re-prompting before they can be judged, and sums can simply be redone.

g6-main-w4-lab.prompt: Your group put Output A above Output B on the trust ladder. Which defence of that order uses a trust signal rather than a preference?
options: A gives a source we looked up and it matched; B states a number with no source anyone can check.
A is shorter and easier to read than B.
A sounds more sure of itself than B does.
Most of our group liked A better than B.

feedback.correct: That is a signal-based defence: it points to evidence - a source that was checked - that another group could check too.
feedback.incorrect: Length, confidence and what your group likes are preferences; a defence has to point to evidence, such as a source that was checked or a match to the task.

g6-main-w4-lab.prompt: Put the five steps of the clinic routine in the order your group should work through them.
items: Read the task and the output at the station.
Assign a verdict and write a checkable reason.
Choose a verification action that fits that type of output.
Rank all the outputs on the trust ladder.
Agree your group's defence of the order and one risk of the least trustworthy output.

feedback.correct: Yes - you can only rank outputs against each other once every one of them has its own verdict, reason and check.
feedback.incorrect: Each output is triaged and given a check first; the ladder compares outputs, so it can only be built after every station has a verdict and reason, and the defence comes last.

g6-main-w4-lab.prompt: Select ALL the outputs that belong near the BOTTOM of the trust ladder, as the least trustworthy.
options: An output that gives a statistic but names no source, so nobody in the group can check it.
An output whose date clashes with the date printed on the station card.
An output that answers a different question from the one the task asked.
An output that matched the original article line by line when the group compared them.
An output that sets its answer out in a neatly labelled table.

feedback.correct: Good - no source, a clash with the station card, and answering the wrong task are all trust signals pushing an output down the ladder.
feedback.incorrect: Low trust comes from signals: nothing to check against, a clash with a source, or not answering the task. A neat table is only presentation, and an output that matched the original belongs near the top.

g6-main-w4-lab.prompt:
Complete the clinic's rule for choosing a check. Write one word in each gap.
A claimed fact needs a trusted ______, but a summary needs comparing back to the ______ text.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the check has to match the output: facts are checked against a trusted source, summaries against the text they came from.
feedback.incorrect: A fact is checked against a trusted source, but a summary can only be checked against the original text it was made from - a website cannot tell you whether the summary matches your article.

g6-main-w5-core.prompt: Layla asks an AI tool what time the school science fair opens. She copies the answer straight onto a poster that goes up in the main corridor. Which risk family is this, and who could it affect?
options: Accuracy risk - if the time is wrong, everyone who reads the poster could arrive at the wrong time.
Accuracy risk - but only Layla is affected, because it is her poster.
