Safety and privacy risk - the AI tool now knows when the science fair is.
Safety and privacy risk - Layla typed a question into a tool that may store what she asks.

feedback.correct: Exactly - an unchecked output is an accuracy risk, and the harm spreads to everyone who trusts the work it goes into.
feedback.incorrect: No personal data was entered here, so this is an accuracy risk - and a wrong time on a public poster reaches far more people than just Layla.

g6-main-w5-core.prompt: Ravi wants an AI tool to tidy up the wording of a party invitation. Before he types his draft into the tool, which details should he take out?
options: His classmate Sara Ahmed's full name
His home address, Villa 12, Al Rayyan Street
His mother's mobile number
The fact that the party starts at four o'clock
The fact that there will be pizza and a cake

feedback.correct: Right - names, addresses and phone numbers identify real people, so they are the parts that create a privacy risk if the tool stores them.
feedback.incorrect: The risk is in details that identify a person - a full name, an address, a phone number. A start time and a menu identify nobody.

g6-main-w5-core.prompt: Match each situation to the responsible-use rule that would reduce its risk.
left: Omar pastes an AI answer about how volcanoes form straight into his science report.
Mei types a classmate's full name and home address into a chatbot so it can write a thank-you note.
Yusuf finds a new AI app online and is not sure whether it is safe to use for homework.
right: Never enter personal or identifying data into an AI tool.
Tell an adult if you are unsure about a tool.
Check the output against a trusted source before you use it.

feedback.correct: Good matching - a rule only counts as useful when it actually reduces the particular risk in front of you.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what could go wrong in each case: a wrong fact needs checking, identifying details should never be typed in, and an unknown tool needs an adult.

g6-main-w5-core.prompt: Put the four steps of the risk-check routine into the order the lesson uses them.
items: Name who could be affected.
Read the scenario.
Attach a responsible-use rule that reduces the risk.
Decide whether it is an accuracy risk or a safety and privacy risk.

feedback.correct: That is the chain - risk, then who, then rule. The rule comes last because it has to fit the risk you named.
feedback.incorrect: You cannot pick a rule until you know what the risk is and who it could harm, so the rule is always the last step.

g6-main-w5-core.prompt: True or false: a mistake in an AI answer only affects the person who asked the question.

feedback.correct: Correct - an unchecked mistake spreads into your work and on to anyone who trusts it, which is why every risk has a who.
feedback.incorrect: Think about where the answer ends up: in a report, a poster or a message, so the mistake reaches everyone who trusts that work.

g6-main-w5-lab.prompt: Your group is the class safety board. Put the five audit steps into the order you carry them out.
items: Plot each flagged risk on the likelihood-impact matrix.
Read each log entry against the rule set.
Write and pitch one rule that would close the gap.
Flag the gaps and name the risk and who it affects.
Circle the highest-priority risk.

feedback.correct: That is the audit order - you can only rank risks you have found, and you only write a rule once you know which risk comes first.
feedback.incorrect: An audit compares practice with the rules first. Ranking comes after flagging, and the rule is written for the risk you circled.

g6-main-w5-lab.prompt: Which of these entries in the anonymised class use-log are genuine gaps your board should flag?
options: A demo prompt was typed in with a student's full name still in it.
An AI answer about rainfall was pasted into a report without being checked anywhere else.
A class photo was uploaded to a tool to turn it into a cartoon poster.
A student asked the teacher whether a new app was safe before using it.
A student checked an AI fact against the textbook before putting it in their work.

feedback.correct: Yes - a gap is a place where practice does not meet the rule, and identifying data or unchecked output are exactly that.
feedback.incorrect: Asking an adult and checking a fact against a trusted source are the rules being followed, not gaps - the gaps are the names, the photo and the unchecked answer.

g6-main-w5-lab.prompt: Match each flagged risk to where it belongs on the likelihood-impact matrix.
left: Real names are typed into prompts in most lessons, and a named student could be exposed to strangers.
An AI sentence is copied into a personal rough draft most weeks, and nobody but the writer ever reads that draft.
One unchecked AI statistic has been printed once all year - in the newsletter sent to every family.
A tool once mis-spelled a group's name on a practice slide, which was deleted a minute later.
right: Low likelihood, high impact
High likelihood, high impact
Low likelihood, low impact
High likelihood, low impact

feedback.correct: Well placed - likelihood is how often it could happen and impact is how much harm it would cause, and they are judged separately.
feedback.incorrect: Judge the two axes one at a time: how often does it happen, and how much harm does it do when it does? Something frequent can still be low impact.

g6-main-w5-lab.prompt: Your board has plotted these four risks on the likelihood-impact matrix. Which one should the class mitigate first?
options: The unchecked statistic in the newsletter, because it reached every family.
Real names typed into prompts, because it happens often and a named student could be exposed.
AI sentences copied into private rough drafts, because it happens most weeks.
The mis-spelled group name, because it is the one everybody noticed.

feedback.correct: Right - the risk that is high on both axes is the one to mitigate first, not the one that is merely frequent or merely serious.
feedback.incorrect: Compare both axes. The newsletter is serious but rare, the rough drafts are frequent but harmless - only the names are high on likelihood and impact.

g6-main-w5-lab.stem: Before any prompt is typed, replace every real name with the words '___'. This closes the gap because identifying data is never entered, so the ___ of a student being exposed drops.

feedback.correct: That is a realistic mitigation - swapping the name keeps the prompt useful while moving the risk down the likelihood axis.
feedback.incorrect: A workable rule keeps the task possible: use a general word like 'a student' instead of a real name, which makes exposure far less likely.

g6-main-w6-core.prompt: Mia wants to use an AI tool to help plan a class assembly. Put the four links of the chain in the order the lesson says they should happen, from first to last.
items: Triage the output as correct, incorrect or unclear
Run a risk check and choose a responsible action
Work out the system type so you know what to expect from the tool
Write a clear prompt to guide the output
answer: Work out the system type so you know what to expect from the tool
Write a clear prompt to guide the output
Triage the output as correct, incorrect or unclear
Run a risk check and choose a responsible action

feedback.correct: That is the chain: the system type tells you what to expect, the prompt shapes the output, the output is then triaged, and the risk check covers the whole process.
feedback.incorrect: Each link feeds the next - you need to know the system type before you can write a good prompt, and you cannot triage or risk-check an output you have not produced yet.

g6-main-w6-core.prompt: Layla is using a learning-based summarising tool on a news article. Instead of "Summarise this article in three sentences, covering only its main argument", she types "Tell me about this". Using the chain from the lesson, what is the most likely knock-on effect?
options: The output wanders off the main argument, which makes the triage harder and leaves more risk of using something wrong
The output stays exactly on task, but the tool takes longer to produce it
The tool stops being a learning system and starts working from fixed rules instead
The triage step is no longer needed, because a short prompt always gives a short output

feedback.correct: Exactly - a vague prompt weakens every link after it: the output drifts, the triage gets harder, and the risk goes up.
feedback.incorrect: The prompt cannot change what kind of system you are using; what it changes is the output, and a drifting output is harder to triage and riskier to use.

g6-main-w6-core.prompt: Omar has an AI-written summary he plans to put in a class newsletter. Which of these are genuine risk-reduction choices, as the lesson describes a risk check? Select all that apply.
options: Taking his classmates' names and phone numbers out of the prompt before he sends it
Checking a surprising fact in the summary against the original article before he shares it
Marking the parts he could not check as unclear and leaving them out until he can check them
Making the prompt much longer, so the tool has more words to work with
Accepting the summary because it is written in confident, well-organised language
Choosing whichever tool gives him an answer fastest

feedback.correct: Each of those names something that could go wrong and does something about it - that is what a risk check is for.
feedback.incorrect: A risk check asks what could go wrong and then acts on it. Length, confident wording and speed do not reduce any risk - confident wording can even hide a mistake.

g6-main-w6-core.prompt: True or false? Once you have written a very specific prompt, you can skip the triage step, because a specific prompt guarantees the output is correct.

feedback.correct: Right - a specific prompt makes the triage easier, but it never replaces it; every output still has to be judged correct, incorrect or unclear.
feedback.incorrect: A good prompt only makes the output easier to check. Miss the triage link and the chain weakens, however carefully you wrote the prompt.

g6-main-w6-core.prompt: Match each link in the chain to the job it does for the link that follows it.
left: Naming the system type
Writing a specific prompt
Triaging the output
Running a risk check
right: Tells you what sort of results you can expect before you start
Keeps the output on task, so it is easier to judge
Decides whether what you got is correct, incorrect or unclear
Asks what could go wrong and picks a responsible action

feedback.correct: That is the whole chain in one table - each link does a different job, and each one hands something to the next.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what each link produces: the system type sets your expectations, the prompt steers the output, the triage judges it, and the risk check decides what to do about what could go wrong.

g6-main-w6-lab.prompt: Put the five steps of a build-and-check task in the order the lesson runs them, from first to last.
items: Triage the output for accuracy against the source
Decide use, do not use, or use-with-changes
Choose a system that suits the task and say why
Assess the risk in the output and choose a mitigation
Design a clear, specific prompt and produce the output
answer: Choose a system that suits the task and say why
Design a clear, specific prompt and produce the output
Triage the output for accuracy against the source
Assess the risk in the output and choose a mitigation
Decide use, do not use, or use-with-changes

feedback.correct: That is build-and-check in order: you build with a system and a prompt, then check accuracy and risk, and only then decide.
feedback.incorrect: You build first and check second, and the decision comes last - it has to be made using both verdicts, so it cannot come before them.

g6-main-w6-lab.prompt: Sara's build-and-check record says: accuracy verdict - two of the three facts match the article, the third cannot be found in it; risk verdict - low, because no personal data was used. Which decision best fits her two verdicts?
options: Use-with-changes: take out or verify the fact she could not find, then use the rest
Use: the risk verdict is low, so the output is safe to use exactly as it is
Do not use: an output with even one unchecked detail has to be thrown away completely
Use: two facts out of three are correct, so most of the output is right

feedback.correct: Use-with-changes is a real third option: the low risk does not excuse the unchecked fact, but one unchecked fact does not waste the whole output either.
feedback.incorrect: A low risk verdict does not cancel out an accuracy problem, and one unchecked fact does not ruin everything - fix the weak part and use the rest.

g6-main-w6-lab.prompt: Match each station in the lab to the piece of evidence it should leave in your build-and-check record.
left: System station
Prompt station
Accuracy station
Risk station
right: A named system type with a reason why it suits this task
The exact instruction you gave the tool, written out
A verdict of correct, incorrect or unclear with a reason you can check against the source
A named thing that could go wrong plus the mitigation you chose for it

feedback.correct: Four stations, four pieces of evidence - that record is what makes your final decision defensible.
feedback.incorrect: Each station leaves its own evidence: a justified system choice, the prompt itself, an accuracy verdict with a checkable reason, and a risk with its mitigation.

g6-main-w6-lab.prompt: Yusuf has to justify his use decision. Which of these actually support that decision, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
options: His accuracy verdict, with a reason he can check against the source
His risk verdict, with the mitigation he chose
The parts he marked unclear in his accuracy verdict, named so someone else can check them
The output is neatly laid out and sounds confident
The tool produced the answer in under two seconds
The output is longer and more detailed than his classmates' outputs

feedback.correct: A use decision rests on the two verdicts and on being honest about what you could not check - not on how the output looks.
feedback.incorrect: Neat layout, speed and length tell you nothing about whether the output is true or safe - that is exactly how building without checking produces confident mistakes.

g6-main-w6-lab.prompt: True or false? Hamad finished the risk station faster than any other station, so that speed is good evidence that risk is his strongest strand.

feedback.correct: Right - you diagnose your strands by how thin or thick your recorded evidence is, not by how quickly you got through a station.
feedback.incorrect: Finishing fast often means thin evidence. Your weakest link is the strand where the evidence you recorded was thinnest, whatever the clock said.

g6-main-w7-core.prompt: Layla planned a lost-property helper. Goal: "Sort the found-items list into categories so items get back to their owners faster." Prompt structure: "You are a lost-property helper. Sort each item into clothing, devices or other. If an item does not fit a category, label it other." Inputs: "a made-up list of ten found items, with no names on it." Risk: "the AI might put an item in the wrong category, so a person reads the sorted list before it is posted." Which one of the five plan parts is still missing?

options.text: The evaluation method - she has not said how she will judge whether the sorting is accurate.
The goal - her first sentence does not say what the solution is for.
The inputs - she has not said what information the prompt works on.
The risk mitigation - she names a risk but does nothing about it.

feedback.correct: Right - Layla has a risk plan but no agreed way to judge accuracy, such as checking the sorted list against a teacher's answer key.
feedback.incorrect: Look again: the goal, the inputs and a mitigation (a person checks before posting) are all there. Nothing tells you how she will judge whether the sorting is accurate.

g6-main-w7-core.prompt: Omar wrote these five lines on his plan sheet for a bus-timetable helper. Match each line to the part of the plan it fills.

left.text: "Help new students find the three earliest buses home after clubs."
"You are a timetable helper. List the three earliest buses. If a time is missing, say so."
"A made-up timetable of twelve bus times, with no student names on it."
"I will compare the three times the AI lists against the teacher's answer key."
"The AI might invent a bus time, so a person checks the three times before they go on the noticeboard."

right.text: The goal
The prompt structure
The inputs
The evaluation method
The risk mitigation

feedback.correct: Well matched - a plan is complete when all five parts are written down and each one does its own job.
feedback.incorrect: Check the last two: the evaluation method says how you judge accuracy, while the risk mitigation names something that could go wrong and the choice that reduces it.

g6-main-w7-core.prompt: Sara says: "My risk plan already says a person will check the output, so I do not need an evaluation method as well." Is Sara right?

feedback.correct: Correct - the evaluation method tells that person what to compare the output against, so without it the check has no standard to judge by.
feedback.incorrect: The two parts do different jobs: the evaluation method sets how accuracy is judged (for example, against an answer key), and the risk plan lowers the chance or impact of a failure.

g6-main-w7-core.prompt: Put the steps of the plan-sheet routine into the order the lesson gives them.

items.text: Read the task card and write the goal in one clear sentence.
Fill the role, task and rule slots of the prompt structure.
List the inputs the prompt needs, checking there is no personal data.
Write the evaluation method and one risk with its mitigation.
Self-check against the five-part list, then submit for the approve-to-build gate.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the goal comes first because every later part has to serve it, and the gate comes last because it checks a finished plan.
feedback.incorrect: The goal is written first, the prompt structure and inputs are built to serve it, the check and risk come next, and the approve-to-build gate is the last step.

g6-main-w7-core.prompt: Rashid's solution sorts a found-items list. The risk he names is: "the AI might add an item that was never on my list, and sound sure about it." Choose the TWO design choices in his plan that would reduce that risk.

options.text: Add the rule: "Use only the items on the list I give you. If you are unsure about an item, say so."
Check the sorted list against the original found-items list before anything is posted.
Make the goal sentence longer so the AI is given more detail to work with.
Give the AI twenty items at a time instead of ten so it has more to compare.
Ask the AI to sound more confident so the sorted list is easier to read.

feedback.correct: Yes - a rule that limits the AI to the given items plus a human check against the original list both make an invented item far less likely to slip through.
feedback.incorrect: A longer goal, a bigger batch or a more confident tone do not stop an invented item. What stops it is a rule that ties the AI to your list and a check against that list.

g6-main-w7-lab.prompt: Bilal's prototype has the task "label each found item as clothing, devices or other". For his pressure test he uses the tricky note "found: a charger and a scarf". The output reads: "devices". Using the lesson's three error-type labels, which error type should he log?

options.text: Missing - the note held two items and one of them has come back with no label.
Wrong - the charger has been put into the incorrect category.
Unclear - the word "devices" could mean more than one thing.
No error - the prompt asked for a label, and one label came back.

feedback.correct: Right - the charger is labelled correctly, so nothing is wrong; what the two-in-one note exposed is a whole item being dropped.
feedback.incorrect: The label "devices" fits the charger, so this is not a wrong answer - the weak spot is the scarf, which never got a label at all.

g6-main-w7-lab.prompt: Bilal now writes up that failure in his build/test log. Choose the TWO entries that meet what the lesson asks for: a fallback branch and a logged reason.

options.text: Fallback: "If a note names more than one item, then label each item on its own line, and if one still does not fit, label it other and ask a person."
Reason: "My pressure test showed a two-in-one note loses an item, so splitting the note before labelling stops items being dropped."
Fallback: "If the output looks wrong, then run the prompt again until it looks right."
Fallback: "If a note names more than one item, then label the first item and move on."
Reason: "I changed my prompt because I wanted the output to sound better."

feedback.correct: Yes - the branch is an if-then that handles the failure he actually saw and keeps a person in the loop, and the reason points back to what the run showed.
feedback.incorrect: Re-running until it looks right, or labelling only the first item, still loses the scarf, and "I wanted it to sound better" is not a reason drawn from the test.

g6-main-w7-lab.prompt: Maya says: "A prototype that always gives a confident answer, even on a messy input, is safer than one that stops and asks a person." Is Maya right?

feedback.correct: Correct - a confident wrong answer gets used without anyone noticing, while a handled failure sends the messy case to a person who can sort it out.
feedback.incorrect: Think about who catches the mistake: a confident answer on a messy input hides the failure, but a fallback branch that asks a person makes it visible and safe.

g6-main-w7-lab.prompt: Put the steps of the lab routine into the order the lesson gives them.

items.text: Copy the approved prompt structure into the prototype slot of the log.
Watch the normal-input run on the board and record whether it met the goal.
Pressure-test with a tricky curated input and record the error type.
Write the fallback branch as an if-then sentence that asks a person.
Log the one change made and the reason it will help.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the normal run comes before the pressure test so you know the prototype works at all, and the branch is written only once a real weak spot has shown itself.
feedback.incorrect: You cannot design a fallback for a failure you have not seen yet: prototype, run it normally, pressure-test it, then write the branch and log the reason.

g6-main-w7-lab.prompt: Four groups pressure-tested the same found-items prototype and each exposed a different weak spot. Match each weak spot to the fallback branch that handles it.

left.text: The note held two items, but only one came back with a label.
A scarf came back labelled "devices".
The output said "maybe clothing, or possibly other".
The note had no item written on it, and the output named an item anyway.

right.text: If a note names more than one item, then label each item separately and ask a person about any item left over.
If the label does not match the item's own words, then flag that row for a person to re-check before it is posted.
If the answer offers more than one label, then leave the row unlabelled and ask a person to decide.
If the input has no item to label, then reply "no item found" and ask a person, instead of guessing.

feedback.correct: Well matched - a fallback branch is only useful when it answers the exact failure the pressure test exposed.
feedback.incorrect: Match each branch to what actually went wrong: a dropped item, a mislabelled item, an undecided label, and an invented item each need a different if-then.

g6-main-w8-core.prompt: Maya is building her signature solution today. Put her five steps in the order the lesson says a build should follow.
items: Restate your goal and your check at the top of your log.
Run your approved prompt structure on the curated inputs and record every output.
Evaluate each output against your check and flag the ones that are wrong or unclear.
Make one change in response to a flag and re-run it.
Log what happened as evaluate -> change -> result.

feedback.correct: Recording every output before you change anything is what lets you prove the change caused the improvement.
feedback.incorrect: You evaluate and flag first, then change one thing: an improvement has to be a response to something you judged against your check.

g6-main-w8-core.prompt: Sami flags one wrong output. Before re-running, he adds examples to his prompt, rewrites the instruction and swaps the input - all at once. The new output is correct. What is the problem with Sami's improvement log?
options: He cannot tell which of the three changes made the output correct.
He should have waited until all his inputs had been run before flagging anything.
He is not allowed to change his prompt once his plan has been approved.
An output that is correct after a change does not need to go in the log.
g6-main-w8-core.answer: He cannot tell which of the three changes made the output correct.

feedback.correct: With three changes in one re-run, the result cannot be traced to a cause, which is why the lesson asks for one change at a time.
feedback.incorrect: The output did become correct, so the problem is not the flagging or the recording - it is that three changes at once hide which one actually worked.

g6-main-w8-core.prompt: Layla says her build followed today's rules. Which of these show she built her solution the way the lesson describes? Select all that apply.
options: She ran her approved prompt structure on the curated inputs she had planned.
She recorded every output before she changed anything.
She evaluated all five outputs, including the ones that looked right.
She invented a new prompt on the spot when the first output looked odd.
She used a classmate's full name as one of her test inputs.
answer: She ran her approved prompt structure on the curated inputs she had planned.
She recorded every output before she changed anything.
She evaluated all five outputs, including the ones that looked right.

feedback.correct: Following the approved structure, recording outputs before changing anything and checking even the outputs that look right are what make a build honest.
feedback.incorrect: Inventing a new prompt on the spot is improvising, not building to the plan, and a classmate's name is personal data that must never go into a prompt.

g6-main-w8-core.prompt: These four lines come from one student's improvement log. Match each line to the part of the loop it is doing.
left: Output 3 labelled a tablet charger as 'other', which fails my check.
I marked output 3 so it would get attention and a fix.
I added a rule to my prompt listing chargers and cables as devices.
On the re-run, output 3 said 'devices' and 5 of 5 were correct.
right: Change
Result
Evaluate
Flag

feedback.correct: A complete loop shows the judgement, the flag it raised, the single change made in response, and the result that was actually observed.
feedback.incorrect: Judging an output against your check is evaluating; marking it so it gets attention and a fix is flagging; what you did to the prompt is the change; what happened on the re-run is the result.

g6-main-w8-core.prompt: True or false: once you have found one output that is clearly wrong, the outputs that already look right do not need to be evaluated.

feedback.correct: Every output is judged against the check, because a subtly wrong output is the one most likely to slip through looking fine.
feedback.incorrect: Outputs that look right can still fail the check - that is why the lesson asks you to evaluate all of them, not just the obvious failures.

g6-main-w8-lab.prompt: Omar runs his finished solution on all six curated test inputs. Inputs 1, 2, 4 and 6 give outputs that match his agreed definition of a correct output. Input 3 gives a wrong label. Input 5 gives an output so unclear that it fails his check. What number should Omar report as his accuracy count out of 6?

feedback.correct: An output that is too unclear to pass the check counts as not correct, so Omar reports 4 out of 6.
feedback.incorrect: Only outputs that meet the definition of correct are counted - the unclear one fails the check, so the honest count is 4 out of 6.

g6-main-w8-lab.prompt: Nadia's finished solution gives a wrong label for one of her test inputs. Which action counts as handling that failure gracefully, as the lesson describes it?
options: Her fallback catches the output and passes it to a person to check, and she records the fix she made and its effect.
She deletes the wrong output so her log only shows results she trusts.
She reports the output as final and adds a note saying AI is sometimes wrong.
She removes that input from her test set so her accuracy count goes up.
g6-main-w8-lab.answer: Her fallback catches the output and passes it to a person to check, and she records the fix she made and its effect.

feedback.correct: Graceful handling means the fallback catches the wrong output, a person stays in the loop, and the fix and its effect are written down.
feedback.incorrect: Deleting the output, presenting it as final or dropping the input all hide the failure - the fallback is there to catch it and pass it to a person.

g6-main-w8-lab.prompt: Rashid tells the class 'my solution is accurate' after showing one input that came out right. According to the lesson, what is his claim missing? Select all that apply.
options: A count across all six curated test inputs, such as 5 out of 6.
A definition of what counts as a correct output, agreed before testing.
Which of the six inputs failed, not just the total that passed.
A promise that his solution will never get an answer wrong.
The names of the classmates whose details he tested it on.
answer: A count across all six curated test inputs, such as 5 out of 6.
A definition of what counts as a correct output, agreed before testing.
Which of the six inputs failed, not just the total that passed.

feedback.correct: An honest accuracy claim is a count across the whole curated test set, judged against a definition of correct agreed before testing, including the harder cases.
feedback.incorrect: No solution can promise it will never be wrong, and personal data never belongs in a test set - what Rashid is missing is a checkable count across all his curated inputs.

g6-main-w8-lab.prompt: Match each question in the three-question risk check to the evidence from a student's lab log that answers it.
left: Is it accurate enough?
Is it clear enough?
Was any personal data used?
right: No - every input came from my curated test set, with no names or personal details.
It matched my definition of a correct output on 5 of the 6 curated inputs.
A reader can tell what each output means without asking me to explain it.

feedback.correct: Each risk-check question is answered with evidence: a count for accuracy, a reader test for clarity, and the curated test set for data safety.
feedback.incorrect: Accuracy is answered by the count, clarity by whether a reader understands the output unaided, and the data question by the inputs being curated with no personal details.

g6-main-w8-lab.prompt: True or false: because Layla's solution scored 6 out of 6 on her curated test set, she can skip the risk check.

feedback.correct: Accuracy is only one of the three risk-check questions - clarity and the personal-data question still have to be answered before a solution is trusted.
feedback.incorrect: A perfect score on a small curated test set does not answer whether the outputs are clear or whether any personal data was used, so the risk check still has to be run.

g6-main-w9-core.prompt: Maryam's team built a homework-reminder helper for their class teacher. It gave the right reminder on all 10 test cases where the team already knew the correct answer, but the teacher had to type every pupil's timetable in again each morning, so she stopped using it. Judging the solution through the three lenses, which statement is right?

options.text: It passes accuracy but fails usefulness, because it does not help the teacher do her real task.
It fails accuracy, because a solution the teacher stops using cannot be giving right answers.
It passes all three lenses, because it got every test case right.
It passes usefulness because the reminders were correct, but fails accuracy because of the extra typing.

feedback.correct: Correct - a solution can pass accuracy and still fail usefulness, because usefulness is judged against the real task the user has to do.
feedback.incorrect: Accuracy is about how often the answers are right, and usefulness is about whether the solution helps the user do their real task - here the answers were right but the task got harder.

g6-main-w9-core.prompt: Match each lens to the test that gives you evidence for it.

left.text: Accuracy
Usefulness
Risk

right.text: Run it on ten examples where you already know the right answer, and record the score
Watch your real user do the actual task they need, using your solution
Check whether any results are unfair, and whether private data could be seen

feedback.correct: Correct - each lens has its own test, so a judgement only counts when it comes from the matching kind of evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Check the criteria card: accuracy is tested with known answers, usefulness against the user's real task, and risk by looking for unfair results and exposed private data.

g6-main-w9-core.prompt: Put these steps in the order the lesson says to refine a solution and prove the change helped.

items.text: Judge the solution against accuracy, usefulness and risk
Choose the one improvement that matters most to your user
Make that change to the solution
Re-test the same known-answer cases and compare with the earlier score
Write the refinement note saying what changed and what the evidence shows

feedback.correct: Correct - you judge first so the change is chosen for a reason, and you re-test afterwards so you have evidence rather than a feeling.
feedback.incorrect: The order matters: judge against the lenses, choose the one improvement your user needs most, make it, re-test the same cases, then record the evidence.

g6-main-w9-core.prompt: Omar re-runs his ten known-answer cases after making a change, and his score rises from 6 out of 10 to 9 out of 10. He writes in his refinement note that the change worked. He compared only the two totals and never looked at which cases changed, so he does not know whether a case that used to pass now fails. Is that enough evidence?

feedback.correct: Correct - the lesson asks for accuracy up AND nothing else broken. Two totals cannot show that: 6 to 9 is the same arithmetic whether three cases improved, or four improved while one that used to pass now fails.
feedback.incorrect: A higher total is not proof on its own. 6 to 9 looks the same whether three cases improved or four improved and one broke, so you have to compare case by case.

g6-main-w9-core.prompt: A team says their change made the solution better. Which of these count as evidence for that claim, rather than opinion? Choose all that apply.

options.text: The score on the same ten known-answer tests went from 6 out of 10 to 9 out of 10
Their partner said the new version looks much nicer
Re-running the cases that already worked showed that all of them still pass
The team felt more confident once the change was made
Their real user finished the task the solution was designed for, which they could not do before

feedback.correct: Correct - evidence comes from testing that someone else could repeat, not from how the team feels about the change.
feedback.incorrect: Evidence has to come from testing: scores on known-answer cases, re-running the cases that already passed, or the real user managing the task. How something looks or feels is an opinion.

g6-main-w9-lab.prompt: Match each position on the risk matrix to the decision the Lab says you should make.

left.text: A risk that is both likely to happen and serious
A risk that would rarely happen but would cause serious harm
A risk that is unlikely and would only be a small nuisance

right.text: Act on it now, before the showcase
Do not fix it now, but have a plan ready in case it happens
Leave it as it is and keep watching it

feedback.correct: Correct - the matrix decides the action: likely and serious means act now, rare but serious still needs a plan, and a small unlikely risk is only watched.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at how the Lab sorts risks: a risk that is both likely and serious needs action now, a rare but very serious risk still needs a plan, and a small unlikely one is just watched.

g6-main-w9-lab.prompt: In 1 test out of 20, Layla's classroom-finder sent a Grade 1 pupil to the wrong building. Her partner says: 'It only happened once, so it is not likely - leave it off the matrix.' Using the Lab's way of sorting risks, what should they do?

options.text: Place it as rare but serious, and write a plan for what to do if it does happen
Leave it off the matrix, because one wrong answer in twenty is not likely enough to count as a risk
Write it down as likely and serious, so that it definitely gets fixed before showcase
Judge it on likelihood alone, because the matrix is about how often a risk happens

feedback.correct: Correct - likelihood and seriousness are judged separately, so a rare risk that could really harm someone still goes on the matrix with a plan.
feedback.incorrect: Rare does not mean safe. The matrix uses two axes, so a risk that is unlikely but would seriously harm a young pupil still belongs on it, with a plan.

g6-main-w9-lab.prompt: A team freezes their version, then on the morning of the carousel they spot one more small improvement, add it without re-testing, and tell the audience what they changed. Does this follow the Lab's rule about freezing?

feedback.correct: Correct - freezing means the version you show is the exact one you tested and judged safe, so announcing a late change does not make it allowed.
feedback.incorrect: Telling the audience does not fix it: an untested change means the solution on show is no longer the one the evidence and the safe-and-fair statement cover.

g6-main-w9-lab.prompt: Before a team can freeze their solution for the showcase, which of these must they be able to show? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Before-and-after results from re-testing with known-answer cases
A check confirming that no personal data is used anywhere in the solution
Each risk placed on the matrix by likelihood and seriousness, with the action they decided
A new feature added after the final round of testing
Proof that there are no risks left on their matrix at all

feedback.correct: Correct - a frozen solution comes with before-and-after evidence, a completed matrix with actions, and a privacy check.
feedback.incorrect: Freezing needs three things in place: before-and-after results from re-testing, every risk placed on the matrix with an action decided, and a confirmation that no personal data is used.

g6-main-w9-lab.prompt: Complete this team's final Lab statement: 'We sorted every risk by how likely it is and how ___ the harm would be. We checked that no ___ data is used anywhere in our solution. Then we ___ the version, so the one we show at the carousel is exactly the one we tested.'
blanks: the kind of data that must not be there
what you do to the tested version

feedback.correct: Correct - the matrix uses likelihood and seriousness together, the privacy check removes personal data, and freezing keeps the tested version the one on show.
feedback.incorrect: The matrix's second axis is how serious the harm would be; the privacy check is about personal data; and stopping all further changes to the tested version is called freezing it.

g6-main-w10-core.prompt: In your pitch you have to justify a choice, not just describe it. Which sentence justifies the choice?

options.text: My sorter uses five rules — one each for plastic, paper, metal, glass and food waste.
I used a rule-based sorter because recycling categories have fixed correct answers, so the rules give the same reliable result every time.
I used a rule-based sorter because my group voted for that one.
My sorter was finished on time and looks clear on the screen.

feedback.correct: A justified choice gives the reason behind it — fixed correct answers suit fixed rules — rather than listing what the solution contains.
feedback.incorrect: Listing the rules, reporting a vote or praising the look all describe the solution; a justification says why that choice suited the problem.

g6-main-w10-core.prompt: Your Term-1 assessment has to show all four strands. Match each piece of evidence to the strand it shows.

left.text: I can explain how a system that follows written rules is different from one that learns from examples.
I made a working prototype that takes an item and puts it into a category.
I ran my solution on six items whose correct answers I already knew, and recorded how many it got right.
I described who might be treated unfairly if the whole school used my solution.

right.text: Understanding concepts
Design and build
Evaluate and use responsibly
Wider effects

feedback.correct: Each strand needs its own evidence: explaining shows concepts, making shows design and build, testing shows evaluation, and thinking about users shows wider effects.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each piece of evidence proves you can do — explain, build, test or think about who is affected — and the strand follows from that.

g6-main-w10-core.prompt: Which of these belong in a 60-second pitch that tells the truth? Select all that apply.

options.text: Name your user and the problem your solution solves.
Give the evidence that your results were accurate.
State one honest limit of your solution.
Promise that your solution never gets anything wrong, so nobody doubts it.
Describe your two choices without saying why you made them.

feedback.correct: A truthful pitch names the user and problem, backs its claims with evidence, and is open about one limit.
feedback.incorrect: Promising perfection is not evidence, and a choice with no reason is only a description — neither makes a pitch more convincing.

g6-main-w10-core.prompt: Admitting one limit of your solution during your pitch makes your work less trustworthy.

feedback.correct: Correct — honesty about a limit makes your work more trustworthy, because your audience can believe the claims you do make.
feedback.incorrect: The lesson says the opposite: being honest about a limit strengthens your pitch rather than weakening it.

g6-main-w10-core.prompt: Put the showcase and assessment steps into the order that makes each step possible.

items.text: Set out your evidence from the term.
Complete the short assessment task on your own.
Prepare a 60-second pitch with two justified choices.
Present to your group and answer one 'why' question.
Write one thing you learned and one goal for Term 2.

feedback.correct: Evidence first so you can draw on it, the assessment on your own before you hear other people's ideas, then prepare, present, and reflect once you know how it went.
feedback.incorrect: Each step feeds the next: you need your evidence out before you can use it, and you can only reflect on your learning after you have presented.

g6-main-w10-lab.prompt: You are leaving 'two stars and a wish' at someone's station. Which wish is the most useful feedback?

options.text: Wish: your station was a bit boring to watch.
Wish: make it better before you show it to anyone else.
Wish (Wider effects): say who might be left out if the whole school used it, and how you would stop that happening.
Wish: I really liked your colours, well done!

feedback.correct: That wish is specific, kind and tagged to a strand, so the person knows exactly what to work on next.
feedback.incorrect: A useful wish names one thing to improve and which strand it belongs to — 'boring', 'make it better' and a compliment all leave the person with nothing to act on.

g6-main-w10-lab.prompt: Every station needs a responsible-use message. Which statements belong in that message? Select all that apply.

options.text: We do not store anyone's name or photo.
Our checker gets unusual items wrong about one time in five, so check its answer before you act on it.
We tested it with items from lots of different homes so it works fairly for everyone.
Our solution loads in under two seconds.
We chose a purple background so the station looks smart.

feedback.correct: Responsible use means no personal data, honesty about limits, and fairness to users — those three statements cover exactly that.
feedback.incorrect: Loading speed and the look of your station may be good work, but they say nothing about personal data, limits or fairness.

g6-main-w10-lab.prompt: Each carousel comment has to be tagged to a strand. Match each comment to the strand it belongs to.

left.text: Star: you explained clearly why your solution follows rules instead of learning from examples.
Star: your station showed a working prototype that sorts an item into a category.
Wish: try it on more items whose answers you already know, so your evidence is stronger.
Wish: say who might be treated unfairly if your solution was used everywhere.

right.text: Understanding concepts
Design and build
Evaluate and use responsibly
Wider effects

feedback.correct: Tagging works by what the comment is about: explaining ideas, building the thing, gathering evidence that it works, or who it affects.
feedback.incorrect: Read what each comment actually praises or asks for — an explanation, a build, more testing evidence, or the effect on people — and the strand follows.

g6-main-w10-lab.prompt: A wish should be kept general and vague so that nobody feels criticised.

feedback.correct: Correct — good feedback is specific, kind and tied to evidence, so a specific wish is a gift rather than a criticism.
feedback.incorrect: A vague wish is kind but useless; being specific and tying the comment to evidence is what makes it helpful.

g6-main-w10-lab.prompt: Put the showcase carousel steps into the order that makes each step possible.

items.text: Set up your station with your frozen solution, your evidence and your responsible-use message.
Present your solution in 60 seconds with two justified choices.
Rotate to other stations and leave strand-tagged feedback there.
Collect the feedback other people left at your station.
Complete your four-strand summary and set one Term-2 goal.

feedback.correct: You can only give feedback once stations are set up and presented, and you can only summarise your term once your feedback is collected.
feedback.incorrect: The summary and goal come last, because they are built from the feedback you collect after presenting and visiting other stations.
